"Forgotten" for Journalists
The documentary "Forgotten," directed by Mehdi Afsharnik, will be screened on Wednesday, September 11, at the Department of Environment, with the presence of department officials, journalists, environmental experts, and activists. This screening, coinciding with the escalating debates over the development of the Sohrab oil field and the relationship between the oil industry and Hor al-Azim, could pave the way for a serious dialogue among officials, critics, and the filmmakers.
The Wednesday screening at the Department of Environment gains even more significance because department officials, experts, and environmental journalists are set to watch together a film that narrates part of the very controversy that has returned to the forefront of discussions today with the Sohrab field case. A film that, on one hand, critiques oil and, on the other, does not align with part of the prevailing environmental narrative; a combination that will likely make the post-screening session as compelling as the film itself.

entry.title: [darvishnameh] ♦️ Trees that become victims of war! ♦️📚@darvishnameh✍️…
entry.summary:
Source: @darvishnameh

♦️ Trees that become victims of war! ♦️📚@darvishnameh✍️ Mangroves—Avicennia, Rhizophora, and in short, all mangrove species—absorb carbon and produce oxygen several times more than any forest habitat we know, and in addition, they are highly effective in bioremediation of water and spawning grounds for aquatic life. But these days, the Qeshm mangrove habitat has become a victim of war, and its shores are covered in tar! We might think this tragedy ends with a few blackened trees! That's not the case at all... That's not what this is about. What has happened is much bigger than a few trees burning and turning black. A mangrove is not just a tree. It's an ecosystem; a living network that much of the coast's and sea's life depends on. When oil enters this ecosystem, it doesn't just stick to the tree trunks; it enters a complete chain of life. And perhaps to understand the scale of this disaster, no explanation is as sufficient as seeing these images. This isn't just oil pollution; part of an ecosystem is being buried under oil. A clip from the documentary "Qeshm Background" by Yaser Arab#حرا_جان_ایران_است#یاسر_عرب #محمد_درویش

🟢 When the sun in Shazand, Arak, comes to the aid of fish! 🟢📚 @darvishnameh1️⃣ Using solar panels in fish farming complexes can have significant benefits; because aquaculture inherently requires relatively large amounts of electricity for water pumping, aeration, treatment, and water circulation.2️⃣ An important point is that in many fish farming complexes, part of the consumption load occurs during the day, coinciding with sunlight; therefore, solar power can be used directly for pumps and aerators, reducing the need for batteries. Also, as explained in the video: the damage caused by power outages at a fish farm can be very dangerous; because stopping aeration, especially in dense ponds, can reduce dissolved oxygen within a relatively short time and cause fish mortality. A solar system with a hybrid inverter and battery increases production security.3️⃣ But what can make this plan more attractive in Iran is designing a low-carbon aquaculture complex with intelligent water and energy management, leading to fish production with a lower water and carbon footprint. In recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), this becomes even more important, as electricity consumption for pumping, filtration, and oxygenation is high.4️⃣ Bravo to those who are pioneers in greening the fish farming industry in Iran.
